OVERVIEW

[1] The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX (PA), and his wife, the Associate Appellant, XXXX XXXX (AA), citizens of China, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 19, 2021, rejecting their claims for refugee protection because it found the claims not to be credible. They allege fear of persecution and harm at the hands of the Chinese authorities because they are Falun Gong (FG) practitioners. They argue that the RPD erred, and ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a positive determination or remit the matter to the RPD for redetermination. They do not seek to rely upon new evidence, and do not request an oral hearing.

[2] My role is to conduct an independent assessment of all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 An exception can apply where the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the assessment of oral testimony, which may attract deference to its findings.2 I have conducted my own independent assessment of all the evidence and arguments in this case, including the audio recording of the hearing. Unless specifically stated and explained below, I have reviewed the RPD decision using the standard of correctness because I find that it did not have a meaningful advantage in the assessment of oral testimony.
DETERMINATION

[3] The appeal is allowed.3 I set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute the determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, namely that the Appellants are Convention refugees in accordance with section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).

ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

[9] In assessing the credibility of the testimony of the Appellants, I am mindful (as was the RPD) that sworn testimony is presumed to be truthful. However, that presumption is rebuttable where testimony features inconsistencies, implausibilities, material omissions, vagueness, or other valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness, and these can be a valid basis for a finding of lack of credibility which can extend to all relevant evidence provided by the Appellants. I am also mindful that the RPD (and the RAD) may draw conclusions on credibility based on implausibilities, rationality, and common sense.
RPD's credibility findings
Inconsistent testimony about reason for using fraudulent passports

[10] The RPD found that the PA's testimony about why the Appellants used fraudulent passports to travel to Canada was inconsistent with the testimony contained in his BOC narrative. When asked at the hearing why he used a fraudulent passport to come to Canada, the PA responded that he used a fraudulent passport because he could not use his real passport to come to Canada. When the RPD asked why he could not use his real passport, he replied that he consulted a travel agency and asked if he could use his own passport, and was told that he was not eligible for a visa because he did not have the relevant qualifications. The RPD asked if there were any other reasons why he could not use his own passport to come to Canada, and the PA responded that there were no other reasons.

[11] The RPD pointed out to the PA that he stated in his BOC narrative that he was afraid to leave China through legal channels as a result of his illegal FG activities,7 and asked why he had testified that he used a false Singaporean passport because he did not qualify for a Canadian visa using his own passport. The PA responded that he did not think his answers were contradictory because he wanted to go to a country that allowed him to practice FG freely. When the RPD sought to clarify his testimony, he confirmed that his narrative statement was correct - he was not able to leave his country through legal channels, by which he meant that he would not be able to get a Canadian visa. When the RPD asked if there were any other risks to him if he left the country through legal means and used his own passport, he repeated that he would not be able to get a visa to come to Canada.

[12] The RPD found that the testimony at the hearing about the reason for the use of a fraudulent passport - that he did not qualify for a Canadian visa using his own passport - was inconsistent with his narrative testimony - that he was afraid to leave China through legal channels because of his illegal FG activities. It found that the response regarding the inconsistency did not reasonably explain the inconsistency, but merely stated that he did not consider the statements to be contradictory, and repeated his previous testimony. The RPD stated that the PA's statement that he was afraid to leave through legal channels because of his FG activities indicates that he "believed leaving China through legal means could put him at risk and it implies knowledge of the [PA's] FG practice on the part of the Chinese authorities."8 It also found the BOC narrative statement to be inconsistent with the PA's testimony at the hearing that the Chinese authorities do not have knowledge of his practice, as well as with his testimony with respect to his motives for using a fraudulent passport.

[13] The Appellants argue that there is no inconsistency. They argue that the two stated reasons given by the PA "cumulatively informed his decision to use the Singaporean passport...that his primary reason for using the Singaporean passport was that he could not obtain a visa to come to Canada...it is very plausible for the [PA], at the back of his mind, to also fear being intercepted by the PSB (Public Security Bureau) when exiting China because he has no way of knowing whether the PSB had become aware of his FG practice in China."9 They argue that, because "this fear was only speculative (i.e. the [PA] does not know for certain whether or not the PSB was aware of his FG practice), it was not his primary reason for using the Singaporean passport."10 I am not persuaded by these arguments. The first problem with the arguments is that they are counsel's submissions, which are not evidence, and they do not reflect the PA's testimony at the hearing. He did not give these explanations when asked to explain the apparent discrepancy; rather he stated that there was no inconsistency. I do not agree. In his BOC (which he confirmed to be complete, true, and correct when he signed it, and again, at the hearing),11 he stated that the need to use extra-legal means (which in this case, means using a passport that was not his own) was because of his illegal FG activities. At the hearing, it was because he did not have the qualifications to obtain a Canadian visa, thereby causing him to use a different identity and passport. In my assessment, these answers provide inconsistent evidence, and I agree with the RPD that the explanation does not reasonably explain that inconsistency. The issue is not about the plausibility of the PA's belief, as the Appellants argue; rather it is that he did not testify to that belief. The issue is the different answers he gave.

[14] The Appellants also argue that the RPD wrongly found that the PA's BOC answer implies that the authorities were aware of his FG practice. They correctly argue that the PA never stated or insinuated that the PSB had become aware of his FG practice in China. When asked at the hearing whether the authorities were aware of his FG practice, the PA stated that he is "not sure." He testified that his only practice in China consisted of private practice in his own home, either alone, or with his friend. He never participated in any group or other FG activities. He agreed that he had never been detained or questioned about his FG practice. There is no evidence that anyone other than his friend and his wife knew he had any involvement with FG. The AA testified that the authorities in China have not looked for them in China since their departure, and have not approached their family members. There is no evidence of any reason the PA would have for concern that his activities had come to the attention of the authorities. His very limited and private FG activities provide no reason why he would need to use a fraudulent passport to exit China. He did not testify explicitly, as the RPD incorrectly stated, that the authorities "do not" know of his practice; he stated that he was unsure. However, his testimony provides no basis for any belief that the authorities did know of his FG activities, or for his testimony that those activities gave any reason for the need to change his identity to travel. I agree with the RPD that his narrative testimony that he pursued an extra-legal exit from China because of his FG activities is intended to convey the impression that there is a risk of knowledge by the authorities of those activities, when no such risk existed.

[15] I find that the RPD correctly found inconsistency between the PA's narrative testimony and his testimony at the hearing, and that the inconsistency was not reasonably explained.

The RPD asked if not being able to tell the truth about the treatment of FG practitioners by the Communist Party was the only barrier he faced to being truthful in China, and he responded that it was the only one.

Further, in assessing the testimony about the PA's knowledge of FG concepts and practice, I am mindful that such examination should not be a knowledge quiz, and that perfection is not required. The purpose of such questioning is to determine whether the knowledge is commensurate with a claimant's claimed experience and practice of FG in their circumstances. The PA's answers to questions were substantially correct and reasonably detailed. In my assessment, taking into consideration the PA's modest level of education, and considering his testimony overall, I find that his testimony demonstrates a level of knowledge and understanding that is commensurate with his claimed history of practice and study.

REASONS FOR DECISION
OVERVIEW

[1] The Principal Appellant, XXXX XXXX (PA), and his wife, the Associate Appellant, XXXX XXXX (AA), citizens of China, appeal a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated April 19, 2021, rejecting their claims for refugee protection because it found the claims not to be credible. They allege fear of persecution and harm at the hands of the Chinese authorities because they are Falun Gong (FG) practitioners. They argue that the RPD erred, and ask the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to substitute a positive determination or remit the matter to the RPD for redetermination. They do not seek to rely upon new evidence, and do not request an oral hearing.

[2] My role is to conduct an independent assessment of all the evidence and decide if the RPD made the correct decision.1 An exception can apply where the RPD had a meaningful advantage in the assessment of oral testimony, which may attract deference to its findings.2 I have conducted my own independent assessment of all the evidence and arguments in this case, including the audio recording of the hearing. Unless specifically stated and explained below, I have reviewed the RPD decision using the standard of correctness because I find that it did not have a meaningful advantage in the assessment of oral testimony.
DETERMINATION

[3] The appeal is allowed.3 I set aside the determination of the RPD and substitute the determination that, in my opinion, should have been made, namely that the Appellants are Convention refugees in accordance with section 96 of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
BACKGROUND AND OVERVIEW OF THE APPEAL

[4] The details of the Appellants' allegations are included in their Basis of Claim Forms (BOCs),4 including the PA's narrative5 upon which they both relied, and in their testimony at the hearing. Briefly, they allege that the PA was introduced to FG in China by a friend who had practiced FG for six months. He alleges that he practiced FG one to three times per week with his friend, and practiced at home by himself on other days (according to his narrative). He offered to teach the exercises to his wife, the AA, but she was not interested because FG is banned in China. At the end of XXXX 2019, his friend told the PA that he heard the Chinese government was cracking down on illegal activities and was especially targeting FG practitioners. When the PA told the AA about this, she insisted that the PA stop practicing FG, but he did not want to give up the practice. He convinced the AA that they should go to a country where FG is legal, and they decided to come to Canada where he could safely practice FG. They allege that they hired a smuggler, who provided them with false Singaporean passports. Travelling with those passports, they travelled with the smuggler to Canada, where they arrived on XXXX XXXX, 2019, and applied for refugee protection shortly thereafter. The PA resumed his FG practice in Canada, and the AA alleges that she started to practice FG with her husband after arriving in Canada. They allege that, if they return to China, they will not be able to practice FG, and that they will be arrested if they practice FG.

[5] Near the end of the hearing, the AA added that she would like to have more children, and that she could not do so in China because of prevailing family planning policies.
RPD's findings

[6] The RPD found that the determinative issue was credibility. It found that parts of the Appellants' testimony were not credible. It found that the PA had not established that he was a sincere adherent of FG in China, and both Appellants had not established that they are sincere FG practitioners in Canada. Therefore, they would not practice FG if returned to China, so they are not at risk of persecution or harm if returned to China. As to the family planning claim, the RPD found that the AA's fear is not objectively well-founded.
Appellants' arguments

[7] The Appellants argue that the RPD erred in its credibility assessment and findings. They argue that the RPD reached questionable credibility findings based on an overzealous examination of the Appellants' evidence and testimony, and found inconsistency where none existed.

[8] As to the claim based on Chinese family planning policies, the Appellants acknowledge in their memorandum that current family planning policies in China do not strongly support the Appellants' contention that they will be persecuted for having a fourth child, and therefore, this appeal should focus on the RPD's findings relating to the Appellants' identities as FG practitioners.6 Therefore, I will not consider the claim based on family planning policies.
ANALYSIS OF THE MERITS OF THE APPEAL

[9] In assessing the credibility of the testimony of the Appellants, I am mindful (as was the RPD) that sworn testimony is presumed to be truthful. However, that presumption is rebuttable where testimony features inconsistencies, implausibilities, material omissions, vagueness, or other valid reasons to doubt its truthfulness, and these can be a valid basis for a finding of lack of credibility which can extend to all relevant evidence provided by the Appellants. I am also mindful that the RPD (and the RAD) may draw conclusions on credibility based on implausibilities, rationality, and common sense.
RPD's credibility findings
Inconsistent testimony about reason for using fraudulent passports

[10] The RPD found that the PA's testimony about why the Appellants used fraudulent passports to travel to Canada was inconsistent with the testimony contained in his BOC narrative. When asked at the hearing why he used a fraudulent passport to come to Canada, the PA responded that he used a fraudulent passport because he could not use his real passport to come to Canada. When the RPD asked why he could not use his real passport, he replied that he consulted a travel agency and asked if he could use his own passport, and was told that he was not eligible for a visa because he did not have the relevant qualifications. The RPD asked if there were any other reasons why he could not use his own passport to come to Canada, and the PA responded that there were no other reasons.

[11] The RPD pointed out to the PA that he stated in his BOC narrative that he was afraid to leave China through legal channels as a result of his illegal FG activities,7 and asked why he had testified that he used a false Singaporean passport because he did not qualify for a Canadian visa using his own passport. The PA responded that he did not think his answers were contradictory because he wanted to go to a country that allowed him to practice FG freely. When the RPD sought to clarify his testimony, he confirmed that his narrative statement was correct - he was not able to leave his country through legal channels, by which he meant that he would not be able to get a Canadian visa. When the RPD asked if there were any other risks to him if he left the country through legal means and used his own passport, he repeated that he would not be able to get a visa to come to Canada.

[12] The RPD found that the testimony at the hearing about the reason for the use of a fraudulent passport - that he did not qualify for a Canadian visa using his own passport - was inconsistent with his narrative testimony - that he was afraid to leave China through legal channels because of his illegal FG activities. It found that the response regarding the inconsistency did not reasonably explain the inconsistency, but merely stated that he did not consider the statements to be contradictory, and repeated his previous testimony. The RPD stated that the PA's statement that he was afraid to leave through legal channels because of his FG activities indicates that he "believed leaving China through legal means could put him at risk and it implies knowledge of the [PA's] FG practice on the part of the Chinese authorities."8 It also found the BOC narrative statement to be inconsistent with the PA's testimony at the hearing that the Chinese authorities do not have knowledge of his practice, as well as with his testimony with respect to his motives for using a fraudulent passport.

[13] The Appellants argue that there is no inconsistency. They argue that the two stated reasons given by the PA "cumulatively informed his decision to use the Singaporean passport...that his primary reason for using the Singaporean passport was that he could not obtain a visa to come to Canada...it is very plausible for the [PA], at the back of his mind, to also fear being intercepted by the PSB (Public Security Bureau) when exiting China because he has no way of knowing whether the PSB had become aware of his FG practice in China."9 They argue that, because "this fear was only speculative (i.e. the [PA] does not know for certain whether or not the PSB was aware of his FG practice), it was not his primary reason for using the Singaporean passport."10 I am not persuaded by these arguments. The first problem with the arguments is that they are counsel's submissions, which are not evidence, and they do not reflect the PA's testimony at the hearing. He did not give these explanations when asked to explain the apparent discrepancy; rather he stated that there was no inconsistency. I do not agree. In his BOC (which he confirmed to be complete, true, and correct when he signed it, and again, at the hearing),11 he stated that the need to use extra-legal means (which in this case, means using a passport that was not his own) was because of his illegal FG activities. At the hearing, it was because he did not have the qualifications to obtain a Canadian visa, thereby causing him to use a different identity and passport. In my assessment, these answers provide inconsistent evidence, and I agree with the RPD that the explanation does not reasonably explain that inconsistency. The issue is not about the plausibility of the PA's belief, as the Appellants argue; rather it is that he did not testify to that belief. The issue is the different answers he gave.

[14] The Appellants also argue that the RPD wrongly found that the PA's BOC answer implies that the authorities were aware of his FG practice. They correctly argue that the PA never stated or insinuated that the PSB had become aware of his FG practice in China. When asked at the hearing whether the authorities were aware of his FG practice, the PA stated that he is "not sure." He testified that his only practice in China consisted of private practice in his own home, either alone, or with his friend. He never participated in any group or other FG activities. He agreed that he had never been detained or questioned about his FG practice. There is no evidence that anyone other than his friend and his wife knew he had any involvement with FG. The AA testified that the authorities in China have not looked for them in China since their departure, and have not approached their family members. There is no evidence of any reason the PA would have for concern that his activities had come to the attention of the authorities. His very limited and private FG activities provide no reason why he would need to use a fraudulent passport to exit China. He did not testify explicitly, as the RPD incorrectly stated, that the authorities "do not" know of his practice; he stated that he was unsure. However, his testimony provides no basis for any belief that the authorities did know of his FG activities, or for his testimony that those activities gave any reason for the need to change his identity to travel. I agree with the RPD that his narrative testimony that he pursued an extra-legal exit from China because of his FG activities is intended to convey the impression that there is a risk of knowledge by the authorities of those activities, when no such risk existed.

[15] I find that the RPD correctly found inconsistency between the PA's narrative testimony and his testimony at the hearing, and that the inconsistency was not reasonably explained.
Use of fraudulent passports and inconsistency with the FG principle of truthfulness

[16] The RPD correctly noted that the main principles of FG are truthfulness, compassion, and forbearance, which are said to be the fundamental qualities of the universe, and the principles that serve as a guide for daily living and practice by adherents.12 The PA testified in his narrative that he practiced these principles in his daily life in China. The RPD asked him how he applied these principles in China, and he responded that, in China, he was able to live his life in accordance with the principles of compassion and forbearance, but he could not live his life truthfully, because that required him to tell the truth about FG and to reveal that the government has been evil, and he could not do so because of the ban. The RPD asked if not being able to tell the truth about the treatment of FG practitioners by the Communist Party was the only barrier he faced to being truthful in China, and he responded that it was the only one.

[17] The RPD then asked how his belief in the principle of truthfulness is consistent with his act of using a false identity document to enter Canada. The PA responded that using a fraudulent passport contradicts truthfulness, but was measured by their wish as FG practitioners to practice FG freely. The RPD found that the use of a false passport at a time when he was in no imminent danger from the authorities was inconsistent with the PA's emphasis on the importance of truthfulness. It found that it is reasonable to expect that a sincere believer in FG principles "would at the very least make attempts to leave the country without resorting to fraudulent means before being forced to act against their core beliefs." It then noted that, when asked about barriers to his application of the principle of truthfulness in China, he did not mention that he was forced to act against this principle to come to a country where he could practice FG freely; he only addressed this issue when directly asked by the panel about the perceived contradiction between his actions and FG teachings. The RPD found it reasonable to expect an individual who claims to be a sincere adherent of a practice to "at the very least have some internal moral struggle with having to defy his core beliefs." The RPD expected the issue would be significant to a genuine practitioner and to have been raised spontaneously by a genuine practitioner in response to the RPD's question about barriers to truthfulness. The RPD drew a significant negative credibility inference with respect to the PA being a sincere adherent of FG in China.

[18] As to the RPD's first finding - that it is reasonable to expect the PA to have made attempts to leave the country without resorting to fraudulent means - the Appellants correctly argue that this finding appears to overlook the PA's narrative testimony that the Appellants first made inquiries about how to obtain Canadian visitor visas, but learned that they would not qualify based on their profiles.13 It was then that they found a smuggler who provided fraudulent passports. It is true that there was no imminent danger at the time, but the issue was not the timing of the danger. Once the Appellants determined that they would not qualify for visitor visas (which themselves would have required untruthfulness), the choice became whether to use extra-legal avenues such as a smuggler and false passports, or to remain in China. The RPD erred in this finding because it is inconsistent with the evidence.

[19] As to the RPD's second finding, I am not prepared to find that the PA is not a genuine FG practitioner because it is not clear that he experienced an "internal moral struggle" about being untruthful when it appears that it was necessary for him to do so to flee China in pursuit of his freedom to practice FG freely. The RPD did not question the PA about whether or to what extent, he had a moral struggle. It is true that the PA did not mention this issue when asked about barriers encountered in China to his principle of truthfulness, but I am not satisfied that it is reasonable to draw an adverse inference from his failure to mention this issue in response to the question asked of him. He had already clearly acknowledged that he had been untruthful by using a fraudulent passport to leave the country.

[20] In these circumstances, I find the RPD erred in drawing an adverse inference because of an inconsistency between the PA's beliefs and his actions in using a fraudulent passport. I find that the use of such a passport does not negatively impact the credibility of the PA or his allegation that he was a FG practitioner in China.
The presumption of truthfulness has not been rebutted

[21] As noted previously, a claimant's testimony is presumed truthful unless there are valid reasons to doubt it's truthfulness. The RPD found that the presumption of truthfulness has been rebutted. It found that the PA was not a sincere adherent of FG in China based on: (1) its credibility finding regarding the PA's inconsistent testimony about the reason for using a fraudulent passport, and (2) its adverse inference relating to the use of a fraudulent passport being found to be inconsistent with the central FG principle of truthfulness.14

[22] I have found that the RPD erred in the second of those reasons. That leaves the one correct credibility finding as the only basis for the findings that the presumption of truthfulness was rebutted, and that the PA was not a FG practitioner in China. While I have found the RPD was correct regarding that credibility finding, in my assessment, that adverse finding does not relate to an issue that is sufficiently central to the Appellants' claims to justify the RPD's findings. Put differently, I do not regard that adverse finding as being sufficient reason, on its own, to rebut the presumption of truthfulness to which the Appellants are entitled. It does not go the heart of the allegations on which the claim is based.

[23] No reasons are disclosed by the evidence elicited to find that the PA has not established that he became a FG practitioner in China. The testimony of the PA that he became a FG adherent and practitioner in China is presumed to be true and, based on that presumption, has been established on a balance of probabilities.
Sur place claim

[24] The RPD also found that the Appellants have not become sincere FG practitioners in Canada. In reaching that finding regarding the PA, it relied heavily on its finding that the PA was not credible with respect to his practice in China, and its ability to import negative findings to the assessment of a claimant's sur place claim. Since it found the PA not credible with respect to his FG practice in China, and as the PA did not provide a credible motive for joining FG in Canada independent of his alleged practice in China, the RPD drew a negative inference with respect to the PA's practice of FG in Canada, and found that he has not become a sincere FG practitioner in Canada. It found that the PA's "alleged practice in China is directly linked to the sincerity of his practice in Canada, and that [his] lack of credibility with respect to his practice in China negatively impacts the credibility of his practice in Canada."15 Given my finding that the RPD's finding that the PA was not credible about his practice of FG in China is erroneous, the adverse inference about his practice in Canada that is based on the erroneous finding about his practice in China cannot stand, and cannot negatively impact the credibility of his practice in Canada.

[25] The RPD found that, while the PA's responses when questioned about his understanding of FG were not completely accurate, he was able to answer most of the RPD's questions about the teachings of FG. However, it found that, while knowledge is an important part of the practice of FG, it "cannot be the sole determinative factor in the face of other significant credibility issues [emphasis added]."16 It found that the PA's level of knowledge is insufficient to overcome the RPD's credibility concerns, and to establish that he is currently a sincere FG practitioner. I have found that the RPD erred in its credibility findings regarding the PA's FG practice in China. There were no valid "significant credibility issues" to be overcome.

[26] Further, in its analysis of the PA's knowledge of FG, the RPD correctly observed that knowledge is an important part of FG practice. The genuineness of a claimant's religious (including Falun Gong) identity may be reasonably questioned if their knowledge of their religion is not commensurate with their claimed experience, taking into consideration their circumstances and the features of the religion in question.17 What qualifies as commensurate must be assessed on a case-by-case basis, as it will depend on the claimant's circumstances and the features of the religion in question. In the context of FG, which is knowledge-based, there is an expectation that a genuine practitioner would make efforts to grow their understanding of FG from the time they begin their practice of FG.18 The RPD noted that the PA demonstrated knowledge about central aspects of FG practice and concepts, including the five exercises and how performing them makes him feel, the concept of attachments, and the law wheel. It noted that he was able to perform parts of some of the exercises at the hearing. However, it found three issues with the PA's answers to questions about FG practice:
(a) when asked about how many repetitions or sets of the movements comprising the fourth exercise, the PA answered that there were eight sets, whereas the instructions relating to that exercise states that the exercise should be performed nine times. The RPD acknowledged that "[w]hile this might appear as a minor detail to a non-practitioner, it is an important part of doing the exercises correctly. The RPD found that learning the exercises and the number of times each should be performed is knowledge that practitioners learn in early stages of FG practice. Given the PA's testimony about how long and how often he had been performing the exercises over the preceding two-year period, it is reasonable to expect that he would know how many times the exercises should be repeated;
(b) when asked about a feature of the fourth exercise about which practitioners should be careful, the PA, after initially saying he did not know, then correctly responded that the hands must be 10 centimetres from the body. However, when asked what would happen if that direction is not followed, the PA responded that he did not know, while the instructions for the exercise state that, if this happens, the energy on the hands will be taken back into the body; and
(c) when asked how many times the hands are taken behind the back when performing the fourth exercise, the PA responded twice. When the RPD asked for clarification, the PA stated that it was twice during the whole exercise, rather than twice in each set or repetition of the exercise. Having listened to the audio recording of the hearing, I observe that the PA's answer was: "Only twice for whole set of exercise four." It is not clear to me whether the response intended to convey that it occurs twice during each set, or twice over the course of the nine repetitions. I do not understand how this movement could happen only twice over the course of nine (or eight) repetitions, since each repetition should be the same as the other. I note that the RPD did not ask the PA about this apparent contradiction. I am unable to conclude that the PA's answer was incorrect.

[27] Based on these errors, the RPD found that the PA learned some FG knowledge and exercises to support his refugee claim, and that he was not interested in accurately learning the exercises; if he were a genuine practitioner, he would pay attention to the details of the practice. It therefore found that the PA did not establish on a balance of probabilities that he became a sincere FG practitioner after coming to Canada, and that he is not a sincere FG practitioner. I disagree.

[28] First, in reading the RPD's Reasons holistically, it is apparent that the RPD's findings about the PA's practice in Canada was significantly impacted by its erroneous findings about the credibility of his allegations about his practice in China. This undermines the RPD's findings about the PA's practice in Canada. Further, in assessing the testimony about the PA's knowledge of FG concepts and practice, I am mindful that such examination should not be a knowledge quiz, and that perfection is not required. The purpose of such questioning is to determine whether the knowledge is commensurate with a claimant's claimed experience and practice of FG in their circumstances. While the two valid errors identified by the RPD in the PA's responses are not trivial given the duration and frequency of the PA's claimed practice and study of FG, in my assessment, in this case, they are also more in the nature of errors in details than errors that indicate a fundamental misconception or misunderstanding of FG principles or practice. The PA's answers to questions were substantially correct and reasonably detailed. In my assessment, taking into consideration the PA's modest level of education, and considering his testimony overall, I find that his testimony demonstrates a level of knowledge and understanding that is commensurate with his claimed history of practice and study.
Conclusion regarding PA

[29] I have found that the PA's testimony, which is presumed to be truthful, is sufficient to establish that it is more likely than not that the PA became a FG practitioner in China. I have also found that the PA's knowledge and understanding of FG principles and practice is commensurate with his claimed history of practice and study. In the circumstances of this case, I find that the evidence establishes, on a balance of probabilities, that the PA is a FG practitioner. In these circumstances, there is no basis for concluding that he is unlikely to engage in FG practice, if returned to China.
The AA has established that she is a FG practitioner

[30] The AA did not practice FG in China. She alleges that she began practicing when she and her husband arrived in Canada in XXXX 2019. While she was able to respond to the RPD's questions about what FG is and about the second exercise, the RPD found that "her responses appeared memorized and rehearsed."19 This also applied to the AA's inability to provide any information about the movements involved in the third exercise, although after stating that she did not remember much about that exercise, she was able to recite the verse applicable to the exercise and its purpose or theory. The RPD also found that the AA's testimony that she had not had time to perform more than the first two exercises since the beginning of pandemic lockdowns in XXXX 2020 because she had an eight-month-old baby (at the time of the hearing) indicated a lack of interest in practicing FG. The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the AA's limited knowledge about the exercises and her lack of interest in finding the time to perform the exercises, and found, on a balance of probabilities, that she is not a sincere FG practitioner.

[31] The Appellants argue that the AA's knowledge of FG was commensurate with the short duration of her exposure to FG, given that she had only practiced for five months before the pandemic and that she gave birth to a baby in XXXX 2020, after which she performed only the first and second FG exercises.

[32] There was limited examination of the AA by the RPD about her FG knowledge and practice. She was able to provide accurate, if somewhat superficial information about FG, its objectives, and some of its concepts, such as righteous thoughts. She was able to describe the second exercise with reasonable accuracy and to describe the objectives of that exercise and the third exercise. I note that FG texts indicate that practitioners are permitted to do the exercises as much as they can, considering how much time they have,20 so I consider the AA's explanation for her limited practice of FG following the birth of her child reasonable. She had only been practising FG for a short period (5 months before the pandemic prevented group practice). Given her personal characteristics, including her modest education, I find that her knowledge and understanding of FG principles and practice, although limited and somewhat superficial, to be commensurate with her claimed history of practice and study. In my assessment of the overall evidence, I find that she has established, on a balance of probabilities, that she is a FG practitioner.

[33] The finding by the RPD that the Appellants are not Convention refugees is wrong in fact or in mixed law and fact, and cannot stand.
REMEDY - SUBSTITUTING THE RAD'S DETERMINATION

[34] The provisions of the IRPA show the legislative intent that the RAD bring finality to the refugee claims determination process when it can do so.21 Having listened to the audio recording of the RPD hearing and having reviewed the documentary evidence and considered the arguments of the Appellants, I find that the central elements of the claims have been sufficiently canvassed so that I am able to make a determination to substitute for the determination made by the RPD.
The Appellants face a serious risk of persecution in China; there is no adequate state protection or internal flight alternative (IFA)

[35] Country conditions documentary evidence clearly establishes that FG practitioners face persecution and possible serious harm at that hands of state authorities in China. I am satisfied that, if returned to China, the Appellants are likely to engage in the practice of FG, and that they face a serious risk of persecution in China based on their perceived political opinion as FG practitioners, which is a Convention ground.

[36] The documentary evidence also clearly establishes that, given that it is agents of the state who are the agents of persecution, there is no available operationally adequate state protection, and there is no IFA in China to which the Appellants could safely or reasonably relocate.
[37] For all the foregoing reasons, I find that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
CONCLUSION

[38] The appeal is allowed. I substitute my own decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
